title: Against slavery
hookLine: slow at first, Emerson came to speak strongly against slavery

cards: An honest thing to say about a man this path has spent weeks with: on the great moral wound of his country, Emerson was slow. He believed slavery was wrong, and said so in his journals.
But for a long stretch he kept mostly to his study and his lectures, wary of crowds and causes and movements. Others moved sooner.
By the usual account, his own wife was involved in antislavery work in Concord before he was. And people who had escaped slavery were already speaking out, at a risk he never faced.
Then something changed, and the quiet man in the study stood up.

teach.b: First, his reasons for waiting. Emerson distrusted joining things. Self-reliance, for him, meant reforming your own soul before reforming the world, and he worried causes could swallow a person whole.
There's something real in that worry. There's also something convenient in it, and later readers have said so plainly. Second, what changed.
His country passed the Fugitive Slave Law, which required people in free states to help return those who had escaped slavery. Now the wrong wasn't happening somewhere else.
It reached into Concord and asked him to cooperate. In his journal he wrote, in effect, that he would not obey it. Third, what he did.
He began speaking in public, and sharply.

teach.h: HE TURNED ON A MAN HE ADMIRED.
teach.b: He turned against Daniel Webster, a statesman he had long admired, for supporting the law.
He spoke for the cause, and he welcomed the abolitionist John Brown to Concord. Whatever one thinks of every choice he made, the careful man had stopped being careful. Fourth, what it shows.
A good person can hold the right belief for years and still keep it indoors. Agreeing silently felt like enough, until something made it impossible. Speaking up isn't being loud about everything.
It's the moment a private conviction walks out of the study, into a room where it might cost you something.

how: Readers of Emerson often study his later antislavery speeches alongside his early caution, as a case of a private conviction becoming public action.

games.q: you're Emerson. you've believed slavery is wrong for years, but you distrust causes. now a law asks your town to help return people who escaped. what do you do?
o: keep reforming your own soul quietly.
speak publicly against the law, even against a man you admired.
move somewhere the law doesn't reach.
games.why: he began speaking sharply in public, and turned against Daniel Webster for supporting the law.

practice: Let your mind go to one wrong near you, at work, at school, in the family: not the biggest in the world, the nearest. Notice the reasons you've given for staying quiet, some wise, some just comfortable, without sorting them yet.
Then picture one plain sentence you could say about it to one person, and hold it.
